Isn't it a fact that that is all that you saw at the top of the church as is recorded in both this paragraph and in paragraph 28 of your most recent statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: It is true that I smoke in the courtyard of the church, and the policeman were around the place where the smoke came from. Some were exactly at the place where I saw the smoke. The others were a little farther away. And this is true. This is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So for sake of clarification, the smoke you saw, the only smoke you saw, was from the courtyard, not from the church building.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Not from the church building. From the courtyard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. So there was no smoke from the top of the church building?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Is it safe -- strike that. Is it accurate to state, then, that you did not see any gunmen at the top of the church building on that day?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: It is true that I did not see. Even if I wanted to, I couldn't see who hit me, who shot me. I had my back towards them, so how could I see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then when you -- earlier in your question and answer session with Mr. Hannis, the Prosecutor, when you stated, "The police were shooting at me," wouldn't it have been more accurate to state, "Someone, that I don't know who, was shooting at me"? Isn't a more accurate depiction of what you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can we have some clarification as to whether it's the person who fired the shot that went into her back or the other shots that occurred during the following half hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you clarify the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. I will try to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask a slightly different question. You cannot confirm that the individual who fired the shot that struck you was, in fact, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: She's never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please, Mr. Ivetic, do not go back to an issue that's already been very clearly stated by the witness, a very clear answer a moment ago that she was shot in the back and therefore couldn't see who shot her. Okay. What on earth could be clearer than that? Now, let's move on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I have time, I'll back in the transcript and I'll see where Mr. Hannis asked her questions, and she said, "The police are shooting at me." So it's not at all clear to me how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. You see, please don't divert attention from the point that I am trying to deal with, which is you've got a very clear answer, and then you immediately court difficulty by asking the same question in a different way when we know the witness's position on this. We know that she didn't see -- at this point in her answers, we know that she didn't see the person who shot at her and struck her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's move on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can I then get clarification from the witness whether, in fact, she could say the person or persons who were shooting at her for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Once again the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. After you were shot and fell to the ground, did you or did you not see who was shooting at you for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, the police who were in the courtyard of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, earlier today -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would like to ask Ms. Sadiku a question specifically. Now, you have told the Trial Chamber that you first felt a pain in your back. The direction that your back was turned towards, what direction was that? Was it in a direct -- could you please give us the direction in relation to the church where you saw the fire and you said you had seen the policemen before? Please answer that question for me specifically. I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was with my back towards the police. My back turned to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Your back was turned to the police, yes, but I related it to the church where you say you saw the smoke. Could you answer that question further and specifically, what I put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police and the church, they were close to each other. They were in the church courtyard. The church building itself was a little farther away. After the church, there was a hill. They were next to the church. The police were next to the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, earlier today I asked you a question, and at page 40 of the transcript, line 16, your response to that question was: "It is true that I couldn't see whether they were pointing their guns toward me or in our direction because they were very far away from us." How is it that you can now state that these police were shooting at you for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Because when I was struck by the bullet, my back was turned to them, so I couldn't see who shot me. But when I fell to the ground, my face was facing the police, and I could see what was happening after that. So for half an hour they shot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that you personally saw the police shooting at you from the church courtyard?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. After I fell to the ground, all the bullets that came came from the direction where the police were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there other structures in that direction? Other buildings, for instance.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No. There were some, but they were further away and they were lower buildings. The highest building was the church, because it was situated on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how far away was that church from where you fell?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I told you earlier that I cannot give you an estimate of how far it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you consider the fact that you saw the persons who were shooting at you for half an hour, would you consider that to be an important fact relative to your statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I don't seem to understand. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: This is a legal question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask this then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Please don't ask her a legal question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why does your statement not state that the police in the courtyard were shooting at you for half an hour? Why is that not in either of your statements, if you so clearly saw it and clearly remember it?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I told you earlier. I have said that I don't know why it is not in the statement. Everything I said is true, and I've come here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the Prosecutor's office in 2001 that the police in the courtyard were shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor failed to put that in your statement. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, page 5, bottom paragraph of that statement says: "When the gunmen saw I was moving, they started to shoot heavily against me. Because of the shooting, which lasted for a half an hour, no one from the house could help me. I was screaming for help, but none could assist me from the house." And then the first full paragraph -- or it may be the second paragraph on page 6: "After half an hour, two of my sisters managed to drag me into the house despite continued firing from the snipers. I do not know if there were more than one gunmen, but I think there were. I believe it was more than one because whenever we saw policemen, they always were more than only one. They always operated together in groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And she has never stated whether, in fact, the gunman was a policeman, Your Honour. In the statement, it's completely at odds with -- it's open to interpretations of both one or the other, and I would think that if she clearly saw it that would be something important enough to be in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe her statement says: "When I was on the ground, I saw around seven policemen near the church. I think they had made a small fire close to the church." That is what she says with respect to actually having seen the policemen, Your Honour, and I'm trying to get clarification, and that's what I've been trying to do for the last several series of questions, because her testimony here is -- is, in my mind, different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you've got a clear answer that she told the Prosecutor's office that the police in the courtyard were shooting at her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that was with respect to the statement in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about when you were interviewed just the other day in 2006. Is it your testimony that at that time you told the Prosecutor that you clearly saw the police in the courtyard shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again - this is for the second time - the Prosecutor refused to put that in your statement? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how -- how can you answer -- or how can the witness answer that question? It's the same question as I interrupted you on a moment ago. How can the witness answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just one other thing you could perhaps assist me with. Where was the point at which you say Mr. Hannis elicited an answer that the police were shooting at her?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could get back to that, Your Honour. I believe -- if it was at page -- my e-court is logged out. I have to log back in to be able to access that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you checking it, Mr. Hannis? Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I haven't been checking, but we are now, Your Honour. But generally when we talked about that topic, I think I asked her: Could you tell the Judges what happened on that day? And then when she stopped at one point, I said: Could you tell them what happened next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't find the reference to saying the police were shooting at her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 13, line 1, seems to make a reference to the police shooting --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 12, actually, beginning from line 20 to 25: "My friend left me crying and I personally didn't know what had happened to me." And then it goes on the -- at 25 and 13, 1: "But when the police saw that I was moving, they started to shoot again at me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So it was an answer to an open question which was: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wasn't a question by Mr. Hannis about the police shooting at her, which was the way in which I think you described it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise if that's the way it was interpreted. I meant in the questioning by Mr. Hannis she talked -- she had testified as to the police shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It couldn't be a more open question. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you don't know -- or strike that. Do you know if there were any armed battles between the UCK/KLA and Serb or Albanian villagers going on in the immediate vicinity of the village where you were located, do you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No. For three weeks -- for the three weeks that I stayed there, I never met anyone with a KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But as far as the surrounding area is concerned, you did not venture outside of the village, did you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Once again, please. Oh, okay. We were scared to go outside. And this was not our village. We didn't know where to go. That's why we didn't leave the place where we were staying. It was a place unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you do not know if there were any villagers from that village that were located outside of their homes surrounding the village, do you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at page 7, paragraph 8 of your Albanian statement from 2001, which is -- one moment, Your Honour. I'm having trouble locating the English version of that. In any event, you talked about the shelling of the convoy. Now, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: You mean the bombing or the shelling? Could you repeat the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you about the shelling. One of your statements talks about a bombing. One talks about a shelling. Could you perhaps tell us which you recall actually having occurred?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: After I was wounded, I was taken to the village of Zahac. I was taken to stay with a family, and after we joined the convoy, there was five or six tractors behind us. A shell fell on one of the tractors. I don't know how well I described this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that is, I believe, page -- page 6, paragraph 7 of the English, and page 6, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S. Now, in your statements, both the 2001 and 2006, you attribute this shelling or bombing, it doesn't matter which, you attribute it to the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you did not actually see who shot or who shot -- where the shell or bomb, whichever it was, came from, did you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the direction it came from, but that day it was a horrifying day. I don't know what to tell you. I don't know how to describe it to you. There were so many people. Everybody was distressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe -- okay. During 1999, the UCK or KLA was operating throughout Kosovo and was armed with a variety of weapons, including mortars and artillery. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Once again, please, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that during 1999, the UCK/KLA was operating throughout Kosovo and was armed with weapons including mortars and artillery?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I never saw or met a KLA man. And how can I give you an answer about what their weapons were? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then, how can you give me an answer saying that the Serbs shelled the convoy when you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I say this because the whole -- all the people who were in the convoy were saying this, and that's what I'm reporting to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, during the -- during the entire time period you were in the convoy, you never asked any Serbian policeman to help you get medical assistance for your injuries, did you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No, I never asked for help because I didn't dare to tell them that I was wounded. I feared what they might think about my wound. I couldn't trust them. That's why I didn't ask for medical help from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, I believe in your statement, in your testimony in the statement, when one police officer inquired about your condition, your sister told him you were handicapped from birth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. Because that day when we were stopped at this checkpoint, police checkpoint, and we were scared -- they were scared that they would take me away. My sisters were scared. And that's why they answered, "This is a handicapped girl. It's the same thing. She was born like that. It's the same thing. Her mother is handicapped as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, do you know approximately how many days after -- strike that. How many days were you in the convoy heading towards the border and Kukes?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Three days, if I'm not mistaken. So that means that on the third day, at 10.00, we entered Kukes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you talk about various checkpoints where persons demanded money from you. Can you describe what uniforms these persons, whom you describe as policemen, were wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: The same uniforms I mentioned earlier. The same colour, police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did these men have any belts?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I couldn't see them because I was lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be accurate to state that from your injuries you were lying down and were you also going in and out of consciousness while this trip on the convoy was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No. During the whole time I was in the convoy I was in pain, lots of pain, but I was -- I did not lose consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can just go back to finish up a couple more points and then I'll be finished with you, ma'am. At page 3, paragraph 1 of your original statement, that's page 2, paragraph 2 of the English, page 2 paragraph 7 of the B/C/S, you talk about an incident involving your brother Halim at a police checkpoint, and in the -- well, first of all, neither your brother or your family took any steps to complain about the treatment of Halim to the police authorities, did you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and simplify it. You state that your brother Halim was mistreated at a police checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. After that incident, neither your brother nor your family reported that incident to the police authorities, did they?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, that incident was never reported by anyone to the KVM mission. Isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm clear now about your question. No, we didn't report it to the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time that this incident occurred, the KVM was on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated that you never saw any KLA individuals, but did you in fact hear about any activities of the KLA, and for the moment let's talk about the -- within the area where your village is located, within that municipality.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No, I never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hear that the Serbian police maintained a presence in the area in 1998 as a response to KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have any knowledge of the fact that in 1998 the police presence in area where your village is located, that this presence was tied to any KLA or UCK activity?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. During 1998, was the Serbian police present either in your village or in the surrounding area around your village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: On the road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during all of 1998, although the Serbian police were in the area, they never came to your home to cause problems for you or your family. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. During 1998, although the Serbian police were in the area, they never came to your home to cause problems for you or your family during that entire time period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No. With the exception of my brother who was beaten up on the road, and then on the 13th of April when they started burning the houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to that time period of 1998, you indicated that the police were on the road. Is it safe to say, then, that there were crossing checkpoints on the road manned by the police?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, there was a checkpoint at Zhabar, Lower Zhabar. That's the place where my brother was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from that one incident with your brother, neither you nor other family members personally experienced any hardships or abuse in crossing these checkpoints. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I don't know, because at that time I was at school, so I did not go past that checkpoint or through that checkpoint. So I don't know whether there were any problems or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have just a few moments to collect my thoughts and my notes to see if I have any further questions, I will then be done with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. General Pavkovic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, when Mr. Ivetic was asking you about the police at the church after you had been shot, during those three weeks that you and the other 6.000 in the convoy were staying in Zabac, other than the police, in that area during those three weeks did you see any other men with guns, farmers, KLA, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No. I saw no one else, just the police. No one else had guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while you were on the ground after you'd been shot in the back and during that half hour that the shooting continued, were you able to see whether the police appeared to be responding to those shots as though they were coming from somewhere else or as though there were some other armed group in the area? If you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, because of this line of questioning. He's asking the witness to speculate. How can she know that? How can she provide the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Fila, that's not quite right, because the question is in this form, "Were you able to see." So it calls for an answer from her own direct knowledge, not for speculation. So it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After you'd been shot and you were on the ground, you were moving and shots continued to come at you. Did the police approach to try and help you?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Ms. Sadiku, that completes your evidence. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it. We wish you well in your recovery and the further efforts that you hope to be able to make to improve your mobility. We hope that these will be successful. You're now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Hadije Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now please make the solemn declaration by reading allowed the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Judges have before them a statement of your evidence and also a transcript of what you said previously when you gave evidence at the Tribunal. So we already have a lot of the material covering your evidence. The purpose of this afternoon is to enable counsel to answer questions either to clarify or expand this or to challenge it, and please don't be surprised if some questions do challenge the evidence you've given. That's the job of the lawyers in the Tribunal under the system that we have here. You know that from your past visit to the Tribunal. The first of the lawyers to ask you questions will be for the Prosecutor, and that is Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you tell us your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: My name is Hadije Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Fazliu, in 1999 were you living in Srbica or Skenderaj municipality?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us the name of your village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Turiceve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you were living there at that time with your father, your brother, and your brother's wife and their four children.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a witness that we're proceeding with under 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The transcripts are marked as two separate exhibits because she testified over the course of two days. They are P2242 and 2243. And her statement, which was tendered as a 92 bis statement during her testimony, is Exhibit P2241. And I would like to tender all those into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are all noted as part of the process, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Fazliu, in your -- in your written statement, you've indicated that your village had about a hundred houses and about a thousand people living in it at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. This was approximately the number of inhabitants, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you tell us that on the 26th of March, 1999, two days after the NATO bombing began, that you and your family decided to leave the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: We went to the village of Tushile, which is 3 kilometres away from my village. Three kilometres approximately. I'm not sure about the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why had your family decided to go to Tusilje?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Because we, my family and the people in my village, we were refugees within Kosovo. We were displaced. We went in various -- we went to various places all the time. We were all the time ready to go somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened on the 26th of March to cause you to leave your village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the 26th of March there was shelling. There was an offensive, an offensive of the Serbian army and police. So we got on the tractor and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you got to Tusilje -- well, first of all, how big is the village of Tusilje compared to yours? Was it bigger or smaller?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Tusilje is a small village. There are hills around it. There is also a mountain there. But there was water there and lumber. We could use the wood in the forest. And there is no main road there. That's why we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your written statement, it's paragraph 7 and 8, you indicate that you had never been there before, but when you arrived you discovered that there were several villagers from other villages who had come to Tusilje as well. Can you tell us what other villages people had come from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: So in addition to my village there were people from the villages of Skenderaj, Klina, Gllogoc. I can't tell you all the villages these people came from. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you know, do you -- do you know why they had come to Tusilje at that time? Did you talk to any of them to find that out?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, we were refugees in March when the Prekaz incident happened. The police came to our village. We went first to Padaliste first, and then we went to other places, we returned home. So for a year we were refugees within our own country. When we returned home, it was only for two or three days at a time. We couldn't stay for longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that answer to be talking about your family and perhaps the people from your village. What about the people from Klina and Skenderaj and Gllogoc? Do you know what their situation was, the reason they'd come to Tusilje on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Because there was an offensive, and people were being expelled, killed. So people were fearing for their lives, and that's why they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraphs 8 and 9 of your written statement, that is the bottom of page 2 of the English and top of page 3, you indicate that after you had been there in Tusilje for three days the police came, and in that paragraph at the top of page 3 of the English, you say that people from Srbica had come because there had been a massacre in Izbica the day before. Did you know that at the time on the 29th of March, that there had been an alleged massacre on the 28th of March in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was in Turkey -- sorry, I was in Tushile, and there was this convoy that came from Izbica, and half of the convoy came there. They were shelled. One woman and two children were killed. I saw the bodies when I went there. And people, because they feared for their lives, they left the places where they lived and they went to Izbica, to Tushile and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But on the 29th of March, what information did you have about anything that had happened in Izbica the day before, on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: The women from Izbica came. They were in shock, and they told me that this massacre in Izbica happened. They told me. And I told them, "Go to this courtyard in Tushile, but the next day we were also surrounded there, in Tushile as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you they give you any information about what happened in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that after the break, Mr. Hannis. Two things -- or three things I'd like to clarify with you, Ms. Fazliu. You say that you heard about the Izbica massacre from women who came to Tushile. Did you meet them on the 29th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I met them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I asked them what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The second question is: Did you actually go to Izbica yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where did you see the bodies you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see the bodies that were killed there in the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be -- it must be a mistake in the translation. And thirdly, you said that you -- or you referred to a massacre at Prekaz. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened in 1988 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's when you date the fact that you were a refugee from, from that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From March. For a year I've been a refugee. Maybe the 5th of March, yes. I was a refugee in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying these points. We'll adjourn now for the break that's necessary at this stage in the proceedings, and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Fazliu, before I continue I want to back up and try to clarify a few things that I wasn't clear on. Judge Bonomy asked you about the Prekaz incident and when that took place. On the transcript it appears as 1988, but in your answer you said you had been a refugee for about a year since March. Can you tell us what year the Prekaz incident happened that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: It was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And another question that came up concerned bodies in Izbica. Judge Bonomy asked you a question about that. I think you said you did not see any bodies that were killed in Izbica in the massacre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 66, line -- beginning at line 5 to line 10 in response to one question, you mentioned having seen one woman and two children who had been killed when the convoy from Izbica had travelled to where you were. Where did you see those bodies of one woman and two children?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw them when I went out of Tushile, and then I can say that I saw those dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where -- where did you see them? Were they on the ground? Were they in a vehicle? Were they along the road?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: They were close to the asphalt road of Turiceve, which divides one part of Turiceve. So they were there. This is that part where the dead bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so I can be clear, what was your information or understanding about when and how those bodies came to be at that location?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I heard about those dead bodies, that there was a shell and it split the convoy of Izbica, so people going towards Tushile. So the convoy was at the same village, close to the asphalt road. And they were split into two, one part in Tushile. I don't know where the other part went because I was inside in Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I understand. In Tushile, you tell us that on the 29th of March the police surrounded the village and came in. The people from Izbica who came to Tushile, when did they arrive there? Was it before or after the police had surrounded and came in?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: It was a day before, in the evening when they arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in your statement, paragraph -- well, second paragraph on page 3 of the English and the second paragraph on page 3 of the B/C/S, you mentioned that after the police came in to Tushile and kept you there for a couple of hours, they separated the men, and about 1.500 of the men were sent to Skenderaj or Srbica town and questioned at the school there. How did you know that's what happened to those men?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw them, my brother, that they were split when they sent us from Tushile, and I saw people there, and they were there. They were -- men were separated from the women, sisters and women from their children. I saw them with my own eyes that they were split.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand that. After they were separated though, how did you know where they were taken and the fact that they were questioned at the school? Did you see that or did you find out about it later?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I learned about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who from?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: My brother, people who had came back. They had told me that they questioned them, and when they were released -- in fact, they were released later, but this happened during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in describing what happened in Tushile that day, you say the police came first and then the military in vehicles and tanks. Later on in the next paragraph you say that after they kept you there for a couple of hours they told you to go to Klina. When you say "they," who was that? Was that the military or the police or both, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: When we were in Tushile it was the police there, and it is a mountain. It is a mountainous area there. We did not see them. But how can I tell you? There were police all along the road, the military, until they reached the asphalt road, and then we continued our road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I made myself clear, but who was it that told you and the other Kosovo Albanian villagers you were with to go to Klina?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No one told me personally, but the convoy had no where else to go. The convoy was not allowed to go anywhere else. It had to go towards Klina, and that's how -- when we started off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next two paragraphs in your statement, you explain how as you were -- as the convoy was heading back toward Klina you decided to go to your home, to your village, and you stayed there for a couple of days without any food, and that on -- the next paragraph, that on the 1st of April the police came, you and some women tried to flee and they caught about 40 of you and told you to go to Klina. Did those police tell you why you should go to Klina or what you were supposed to do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: When returned on the 29th from Tushile. I -- the road goes through Turiceve, and I was with my brother's wife, the three children, their three children. There was no one else there. We stayed in a garage of my home. There were other people whom I didn't know of. It was raining. It was bad weather. After two days the military came into our houses, to the burnt houses. We had to leave, and it was about hundred to 150 metres that the police surrounded us and asked us to stop. We stopped. They surrounded us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please. Please. You were asked quite a specific question, which was did the police tell you why you should go to Klina or what you were supposed to do when you got there? Now, can you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they did not tell us. We were just told to go toward the road to Klina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I should advise you that your written statement and your prior testimony from the Milosevic trial are in evidence in this case, and that's the reason I may be seeming to skip over some parts that may be important for you. But do understand that that evidence is in evidence in this case. Now, you mention in that paragraph on page 3 of the English, the next to the last paragraph on the page, and in the B/C/S the fourth page [sic] down on page 3, you mention that three people were killed in your village that day. What do you know about that as far as who was killed, how they were killed, by whom?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: On that day these people were killed in the village of Turiceve. On that day I just heard about them. After I returned there, they were at the same place. Their bodies were at the same place. And one of them was from another village. I can't remember the name. And -- but the family of one of the people was in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it men or women; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: They were all men, young people. One was a young person. The others were old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph -- well, in the English page 4, starting in the fourth paragraph, and in the B/C/S on page 4 with the second paragraph for the next four or five paragraphs, you describe the rest of your exodus out of Kosovo; that first you went to Klina on foot, from Klina by truck to Volujak, and the rest of the way on foot to Gjakova, and eventually to the border crossing at Qafa e Prushit. I hope my pronunciation can be understood.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did I correctly describe the -- if we could put an exhibit up -- well, if we could have P615, which is the Kosovo atlas, and at page 17 first of all. Ms. Fazliu, I'm going to ask you to look at a map that will appear on your screen shortly. And -- yes, if we could scroll down a little further. That's good. Do you -- do you recognise the area that's depicted on that map on the screen in front of you? Do we need to enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, no need to enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see your village there on the map, Turicevac? I think we need to scroll down now a little bit since we've enlarged it.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think when we enlarged, we lost it. I'm sorry, could we move the map down. Thank you. A little farther, please.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. I can see Turiceve now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a little farther, please. There's one other place I would want to see, if we could go -- farther. Move the map to the left. I said that wrong. Could we move the map to the right. And move down slightly. A little farther so we can see Klina at the bottom. Thank you. Now, do you see your village? I'm going to ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- to help you. If you can use a pen there, you can touch the screen and actually draw on the screen. If you could do that for us. Would you please circle your village of Turicevac?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Turiceve is here, in that part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Tushile, where you went to on the 29th, do you see that on the map? And if so, could you draw a circle around it as well?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, Tushile can be in that part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then could you draw a circle around Klina for us, where you went to after Tushile?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a screen shot of that then save it as the next IC.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could, when we're ready, if we can move south on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the usher back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the map can you now see Volujak? Or please pronounce it for me.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Volujak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't need to draw a circle on that just yet. I would like to go to another map now. If we could go to page 22 of the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're going to show you another map. And I think if we could go -- yes, to the top of the map along the railroad track. And that's -- that's good. Ma'am, can you see Volujak on this map?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Volujak is at the entry, exit to Klina, some kilometres away, probably three to four, up to five kilometres maximum. Volujak is here. Volujak is at number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And could we shrink the map? I would like to show a larger area on this map before I ask her to mark anything. And you see Gjakova on this map?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you use the pen to draw a circle around Volujak and Gjakova for us.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a screen shot and save that as IC, the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit IC12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally one more, if we could. It's page 21 of the Kosovo atlas. I hope. Yes. If we could go farther south on the map. And then to the east. To the -- yes. All right. I'm sorry, I am afraid this doesn't show what I hoped to show. But regarding the point where you crossed the border into Albania, you mentioned that you had followed the people who were leaving from the Gjakova area because you believe they would know the shortest way out of town to get to the border; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that on the last part of your journey you had to climb a very steep hill, and the old and the sick people had to be left behind when you got there. Do you know what happened to the old people and the sick people from your convoy who couldn't go up the steep hill?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: As far as this convoy, the wife of my uncle and we -- we couldn't go any further because we couldn't get any help, and then the other -- the other people came after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, if I could show the witness Exhibit P18. Ma'am, can you recognise what area is shown on that map?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's Gjakova, Qafa e Prushit, the part here that I can see, that I travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see on that map where -- where you started from in your village, went to Tushile, Klina, Volujak, Gjakova and to Qafa e Prushit? Are all those depicted on that map?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. We will proceed in this order: General Lukic, General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Fazliu. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic we represent the Defence of Mr. Lukic before this Tribunal. I'm going to try and ask concise questions, and therefore I'd like to ask you to give concise answers for us to perhaps be able to get through the cross-examination by the end of the day. Can you hear me? Can you understand the interpretation that you're receiving?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were born in the village of Turicevac, and that's where you lived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked in the book shop in Prizren; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you work in the book shop in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I worked there for about six years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would kindly ask for the witness to sit closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Fazliu, it would be helpful if you could come a little closer to the microphone. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me up until what date you worked in the book shop in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: You mean the date or the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The year will do.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I worked there until 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you didn't work after 1989, did you in 1998 and 1999 move around on roads outside the village in which you lived? I apologise, but I did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: When I needed to go somewhere else for my personal needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you in travelling along those roads come across any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. The normal police were there. In those years I have not come across any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you have any problems at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: At that time, in fact, I went out very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you come across any blockades organised by the KLA in 1998 and 1999 along those roads?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, I have not met or had any knowledge of that, because we left our homes -- until we left our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you left your home in March 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you say you left your home because of the Jashari incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I was not aware of the case of Jashari at the time. The police came from Klina to the part where I live, and then I learned about it the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the police came to your village, what happened?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: On 5 March when the police came, they stopped at Koder of Broj. We left because there were police with heavy armament, and that's why we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the police did not in fact enter your village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the day -- on that day the police entered the village, because I live closer to Broj, and women and children were -- remained at the Broj in Turiceve and the police stopped them there, but we left in the direction of Padalishte in another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how far is Padaliste from your own village?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: It was about 12 to 13 kilometres. The road of Mitrovica and Peja. But where I am, it is not an asphalt road. It is a very small street, not many kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 on page 2 of the English version, or paragraph 3 on page 2 of the Albanian version, or paragraph 4 on page 2 of the B/C/S, you speak about the KLA, and you say the following: "During the war in 1999, there were people from this village who were members of the KLA. They had headquarters in the village which was situated at the school. I don't know how many there were because people were joining all -- joining up all the time." Would 2.500 KLA members be about the right figure?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. I don't know about any figures, because I was not at the school to see them. I don't know how many there were, but I know that there were some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did children go to school at that time?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: The school in the place where I lived was interrupted a year ago. I told you the cases. We were refugees. There were no schools. We could stay -- I was able to stay two -- from two to three days at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that from time to time you would go to your own home and then leave?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: When I left I was not at home for three months. Not only me, but every other member of the family did so. I was sheltered in Padalishte. We returned after three to four days, and we could not -- I could not have stayed at home. I tried to stay at home, but I was not able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the reason for you not being able to stay in your own house the conflict between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: At the time we are talking about in 1998, there was no KLA at the school in Turiceve. I told you about the case of Prekaz. I was not aware that the KLA existed. This happened afterwards, some months after, after several months. Now I can't recall exactly how many months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that in 1998 and 1999 that there was an attack launched by KLA members against police checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, I have not heard about police checkpoints. There were police checkpoints, but I did not hear that there were attacks against those checkpoints, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you weren't there. You had to have been somewhere. Where were you from March 1998 onwards?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I was in Padalishte, and I told you that we could not leave the area. Then we went to Mitrovica, into a quarter there in the suburbs. We remained there for a long time, but we could -- was not allowed to go anywhere else. We had to shelter somewhere because we had no possibility to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you say that in 1999 you weren't in your village either.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I'm telling you that we were away because of the offensives. We had no place where to stay in our homes because there were police checkpoints in Broj and Turiceve. They were firing at us. They were firing at everything they could see. We had no place where to stay at our homes. The schools was not -- the schools were not operating for a year, even after the war. Even in the 1998 there was no school in Turiceve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was the KLA in your village in 1999 or the police? Why weren't you able to stay in your village? Because of which?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Because of the police. Because when they were deployed on the 5th of March, 1998, a relative of mine was killed on the same day, and we had to stay for a month or two in Broj. So we were scared to remain in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is your testimony today that in the same village there were both the KLA with their headquarters there as well as the police?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Later -- the army came later. The checkpoints were removed in Turiceve, in Broj, and then the army -- the police checkpoints were in Jashanice. We were offered ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems from the interpretation that you were offered something. By whom and what was offered?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. I said we were close. We were very close. I didn't say "offered." I said we were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Close to what?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I personally am not understanding the question. Jashanice is close to Turiceve. Jashanice is not very far. Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you to clarify. Perhaps we had a problem with interpretation, but I believe it is clear now. Between Jashanice and Turicevac, was there an area in 1999 that was in the hands of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: This area was in the hands of Serbs from 1998 to 1999 when we left. The area was in the hands of Serbs all the time until we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, to the best of your knowledge, the area around your village was not under the authority of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: The road to Klina, Skenderaj, until -- to my village, to Kline and Turiceve there were Serb forces deployed in Turiceve. There was a police checkpoint. We call it Koder e Brojes. It is the entire village as it can be seen. From there you can see Turiceve and the hills. It is a very high hill there. And there were also checkpoints at Jashanice, but I don't know where the checkpoints were at Jashanice. I've just heard about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, that isn't an answer to the question, Ms. Fazliu. The question was whether any part of the area around your village was under the authority of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was a short time that the KLA was there. As I've told you, I don't know when they left. I can't remember the date when the forces left the Koder e Brojes until the last offensive, when they torched the villages and then we left for Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason you're being asked these questions is because in your statement you say that the KLA had a headquarters in the village, and Mr. Lukic wants to know what period they were active in your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last month, because in the village of Turiceve they were there for a very short time. I don't know for what period, how long this period lasted, because I haven't been in Turiceve. I don't know how long the KLA was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is your village within the Cicavica area?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What area is your village in, then, what region?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: In the region of Drenica, but it's not on the part of Cicavica. It is on the part of Kline and it is included in the Dukagjin area. Between Skenderaj and Kline.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the entire region of Drenica in 1998 and in 1999, were the KLA forces present in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, there weren't many forces. I just can tell you only about the part where I live, because Drenica covers a larger area. It includes municipalities. And I can tell you only about the territory where I live. I don't know about the other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the English page 2, the last paragraph, as well as the first paragraph on the third page, in the Albanian, page 3, paragraph 2, and in the B/C/S, page 2, the last paragraph. There you state that you stayed in a tent in Tushile and that you spent three days there and that the forces arrived on the 29th of March, 1999, at 8.00 a.m. "They came on foot and they surrounded us. As they approached, they were shooting at us." Was anyone killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen many injured. One of them was bloodstained. I haven't seen any other -- I haven't seen any dead people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you didn't mention anyone being wounded or injured in that incident.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Because there was a time when we suffered traumas even after the war. And it's not that I have not told them exactly what I saw, but it is as far as I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to another topic. In the English this is page 3, paragraph 3, in the Albanian this is page 3, paragraph 4, in the B/C/S, page 3, paragraph 2. There you mention 1.500 men who were separated from their families and sent to Srbica where they were questioned in the school building. How long did those men stay in the school building?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw people there. I can tell it to you approximately. It can be longer. I can tell you when they separated, my brother and his son from us, and they sent us in the direction of Skenderaj. I had no other contact with them on the day I left. I learned about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you learn it from at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: When I returned from Albania I learned about it, because all the time I did not know what happened to my family because the family was separated. I didn't know whether they were alive. So these -- I learned about it only after the completion of the war. It was only then when I learned things about my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You live with that brother and his family, don't you?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I've lived with them, but not anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly have not understood clearly that they were -- they were separated at that stage and you didn't see them again until after the war? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about my family here, my own family. I did not see them until I returned after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but does that include your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's includes my brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to that question was yes, that that includes your brother, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard "jo" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I heard "jo," which I thought was "no." I mean, that's why I'm asking. The interpreter has interpreted it as yes, that includes my brother, but the answer I heard was "jo." Now could we have that clarified. When the 1.500 men were separated from their families, when did you next see your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw my brother only after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must say I didn't get that impression from the presentation of the evidence. Should I have picked that up, Mr. Hannis, from the statement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I asked her specifically when she learned from her brother about the fact that they had been questioned at the school. Just that it happened but not when she learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if these questions are really helping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify whether her brother is alive or not. I think that we have the answer now that he is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also have no knowledge of any of the 1.500 being killed that day they were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: I heard about it only I returned that there were some young men, and there were eight young men, and I know them personally, when they were separated, because everybody then left for their homes, and I heard that they were killed. This thing I know for sure. I don't know any further details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, I have to ask myself why you ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I've been misled by this statement we received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say anybody was killed. If I was defending Mr. Lukic, I think I'd be content with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Bear with me, Your Honour, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're finished with that subject, I have one question on it for the witness. Have you ever seen any of these eight young men since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They belonged to my mother's family, and I know them personally because they belong to my family. I know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But have you seen any sign of any of them since the day they were separated from the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not seen them. These were people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't know how to proceed with these kind of statements, because I really feel that I've been misled. We can't find this kind of data in these statements, and I'm not able to proceed based on the statement I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's such a vague statement as it exists from the Prosecution that it's really impossible to imagine any significant point being drawn from it until you start asking for more details and the details start get filled out. Is that what you want? I mean, the Prosecution had even failed to show to me, until you started asking questions, that these people didn't return until after the war. I thought they had returned the following day and told the story to the witness, and I can't see how that would be much of a crime for anyone to face here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I probably have one more question and I'll finish after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Carry on with that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the English page 5, paragraph 1, in the Albanian page 5, paragraph 4, in the B/C/S, page 4, paragraph 5 you state there: "We left Djakovica and started moving towards the border crossing of Qafa e Prushit. We crossed the border on the same day of the 4th of April, 1999. On the way from Djakovica to Krajnica [phoen], there were many soldiers and everyone of us tried to take as good care as possible of their families -- of our families." What soldiers were there with their families?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand it to say that there were soldiers there with their families. I understand it to say the witness was talking about taking care of their own families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Along the way there were many soldiers, and everyone tried to take care of their respective families." That's why I wanted the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What soldiers and what families?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU
utterances.text: Here it is a question of everybody's families. Like I about my own family, other people about their own families. I did not say I saw soldiers and their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "Nothing happened to us on this part of the journey."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shouldn't explore any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, it's quite clear here that the immediate reason for movement at that point is NATO, fear of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now, does any other counsel have questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll resume that on Monday, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably, Your Honour. It depends on the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For scheduling purposes, could we get a rough idea from the remaining Defence counsel how long cross-exam might take, to know when to have the second witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how many more Defence counsel have to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have to consult with my colleagues, but we'll need perhaps quarter of an hour, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Cepic, how long will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, up to 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Hannis, you certainly need some other witnesses here on Monday, and it looks as though they should be here first thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Fazliu, I'm afraid we have to interrupt your evidence at this point and you will have to return to complete it on Monday. The evidence will commence at 9.00 on Monday, so you need to be back in time to start your evidence then. You should not be here for long. Sometime fairly early in the morning you'll be free of the court. Meanwhile, until then, I have to require that you do not, I stress not, discuss your evidence with anyone, and that means either the evidence you've given or any evidence that you are likely to give on Monday. So when you're talking to people, as I'm sure you will be over the weekend, which I hope you enjoy, please keep off the subject of your evidence. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Well, we'll adjourn now and shall resume at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24
